tier_justification: That rewriting is unsound under a non-monotone context is the motivation for frozen positions in rewriting logic; this is the precise, signature-generic form with an explicit countermodel.
plain_claim: For every signature with decidable equality, profile P and context f(pre, _, post) whose hole position pre.length is not declared mono, the explicit Bool model flipModel f pre.length satisfies LeRefl, LeTrans, MonoAt P and KerAt P, makes x0 <= x1 true, and makes f(pre, x0, post) <= f(pre, x1, post) false.
statement: (in the scope of `variable {Op : Type}`) theorem monoCong_refuted_at_nonMono [DecidableEq Op] (P : Profile Op) (f : Op) (pre post : List (Term Op)) (h : P f pre.length ≠ .mono) : LeRefl (flipModel f pre.length) ∧ LeTrans (flipModel f pre.length) ∧ MonoAt P (flipModel f pre.length) ∧ KerAt P (flipModel f pre.length) ∧ (flipModel f pre.length).le (flipVal 0) (flipVal 1) ∧ ¬ (flipModel f pre.length).le (eval (flipModel f pre.length) flipVal (.app f (pre ++ .var 0 :: post))) (eval (flipModel f pre.length) flipVal (.app f (pre ++ .var 1 :: post)))  -- flipModel f i : carrier Bool, le a b := (a = true → b = true), interp g args := if g = f then !(args.getD i false) else false; flipVal n := (n != 0)

non_claims: It does not say that every rewrite under a non-mono position is false in every model; it exhibits one model (and one pair of facts) per position.

It does not say that the operators of a real IR declared equality-only are non-monotone; the countermodel is a two-point Bool model, not a compiler semantics (see pickMin_monoCong_counterexample for an outcome-set instance).
Positive control: at a position declared mono the one-sided step is sound in every model satisfying MonoAt P, in particular in every model satisfying the four laws (monoCong_sound_at_mono).

Escape hatch (two-sided rewriting at eqOnly positions): when P f pre.length = .eqOnly and the premise is strengthened from x0 <= x1 to mutual refinement (x0 <= x1 and x1 <= x0), the step is sound in every model satisfying MonoAt P and KerAt P (Toy.DirCC.eqCong_sound_at_nonOpaque).

Escape hatch (contravariance): the countermodel flipModel negates the hole argument, which is anti-monotone, and in it the reversed conclusion f(pre, x1, post) <= f(pre, x0, post) holds (Toy.DirCC.flipModel_reversed_conclusion). Anti-monotone modalities and a contravariant congruence rule are not modelled; the theorem does not rule out such a rule being sound for operators that satisfy an anti-monotonicity law.
The countermodel is antisymmetric (Toy.DirCC.flipModel_antisymm): the refutation applies within partial-order models too.

plain_claim: For every signature with decidable equality and profile P, a checker policy (which congruence rule is allowed at which modality) is sound for all models satisfying LeRefl, LeTrans, MonoAt P and KerAt P exactly when it allows one-sided congruence only at positions P declares mono and two-sided congruence only at positions P does not declare opaqueArg.

tier_justification: Concrete instances of the refutations in a set-of-outcomes model.
plain_claim: In the set-of-outcomes model (outcome lists ordered by reverse inclusion: t refines s iff every outcome of t is one of s), which satisfies all four laws for oProfile: committing to the least outcome (pickMin, declared eqOnly) is not monotone — [1] refines [0,1] but pickMin [1] = [1] does not refine pickMin [0,1] = [0] — and committing to the first-listed outcome (pickFirst, declared opaqueArg) does not respect mutual refinement — [0,1] and [1,0] refine each other but [1] does not refine [0]; the permissive checker accepts both steps and the standard checker rejects both.
statement:

theorem pickFirst_eqCong_counterexample : LeRefl oModel ∧ LeTrans oModel ∧ MonoAt oProfile oModel ∧ KerAt oProfile oModel ∧ FactsHold oModel oVal [(.var 0, .var 2), (.var 2, .var 0)] ∧ check Policy.permissive oProfile [(.var 0, .var 2), (.var 2, .var 0)] (.congEq .pickFirst [] [] (.fact 0) (.fact 1)) (.app .pickFirst [.var 0]) (.app .pickFirst [.var 2]) = true ∧ check Policy.standard oProfile [(.var 0, .var 2), (.var 2, .var 0)] (.congEq .pickFirst [] [] (.fact 0) (.fact 1)) (.app .pickFirst [.var 0]) (.app .pickFirst [.var 2]) = false ∧ ¬ oModel.le (eval oModel oVal (.app .pickFirst [.var 0])) (eval oModel oVal (.app .pickFirst [.var 2]))  -- oVal n := [[0, 1], [1], [1, 0]].getD n []; Policy.permissive allows both rules at every modality
nonvacuity_witness: The two counterexample theorems are closed statements about concrete instances.
non_claims: Genuine (nondeterministic) choice operators in this model — choose (union) and add (independent sums) — are monotone; the failures are for operators that commit to one outcome by a deterministic rule.

pickMin models a deterministic resolution of nondeterminism of the kind an implementation of freeze might perform; it is not LLVM's freeze, which is nondeterministic and is not modelled in this outcome model.

pickFirst fails two-sided congruence only because oModel represents outcome sets as lists, which are not quotiented ([0, 1] and [1, 0] refine each other but differ); over outcome sets proper, mutual refinement is equality and a representation-dependent operator such as pickFirst is not definable.

Missing operator arguments are read as [].

tier_justification: LLVM's freeze semantics already forbids duplicating freeze; this mechanizes the hash-consing consequence for a toy freeze over poison.
plain_claim: With x poison, `let a := frz x; a + a` inlines to `frz x + frz x`; hash-consing that term merges the two identical frz nodes into one table node, and the table cannot produce the outcome 1 while `frz x + frz x` read as a tree (independent choices) can. So reading the merged node back as the duplicated tree asserts a false refinement: `frz x + frz x` does not refine `let a := frz x; a + a`. For this pair the converse refinement holds in every environment: `let a := frz x; a + a` refines `frz x + frz x` (`Refines letProg dupProg`, the last conjunct of `dup_vs_let_hashcons_counterexample`).
statement: theorem dup_vs_let_hashcons_counterexample : inline letProg = dupProg ∧ hashcons [] dupProg = ([.var 0, .frz 0 0, .add 1 1], 2) ∧ indep poisonEnv dupProg (some 1) ∧ ¬ hcSem poisonEnv dupProg (some 1) ∧ ¬ indep poisonEnv letProg (some 1) ∧ ¬ Refines dupProg letProg ∧ Refines letProg dupProg  -- note: Refines tgt src takes the target first
nonvacuity_witness: The counterexample is a closed statement about letProg, dupProg and the all-poison environment.
non_claims: It does not show that hash-consing (merging) freeze nodes is wrong as a compilation step: for this pair the shared program refines the duplicated one (Refines letProg dupProg). The failure is identifying the two, i.e. reading the merged node back as the duplicated tree.

tier_justification: Giving each nondeterministic instance a unique identity is the discipline LLVM's freeze semantics and Cranelift's non-deduplicated side-effect nodes follow; this states it as a semantics-preservation theorem for hash-consing.
plain_claim: For every program t whose frz occurrences carry pairwise distinct tags (UniqueTags) and every environment, the hash-consed node table of the inlined program `inline t` has exactly the independent-choice outcomes of t.
statement: theorem hashcons_inline_sound_of_uniqueTags (ρ : Nat → Val) (t : Tm) (hu : UniqueTags t) (v : Val) : hcSem ρ (inline t) v ↔ indep ρ t v  -- where hcSem ρ t v := ∃ c : Nat → Nat, (evalTbl c ρ (hashcons [] t).1 []).getD (hashcons [] t).2 none = v (one choice per table node) and UniqueTags t := ((frzOccs t).map Prod.fst).Nodup

hypotheses.purpose: copies produced by inlining share a tag, distinct source occurrences do not

nonvacuity_witness: letProg (one frz occurrence) has unique tags and inlines to frz0 x + frz0 x.
non_claims: Tags must be assigned to the source program before inlining; the theorem says nothing about programs whose tags were assigned after duplication.
It concerns hash-consing only; e-class merging by rewrites is not modelled.
Only freeze over poison is nondeterministic in the language; other nondeterministic or effectful operators are not covered.

hcSem evaluates each table node once and shares its value among all uses (DAG semantics). The theorem is about that table semantics and says nothing about code generated from the table. Reading the table back as a tree duplicates shared frz nodes and is unsound even when the source has unique tags: for letProg (unique tags) the table of the inlined program is that of dupProg, and dupProg read as a tree does not refine letProg (Toy.DirCC.Dup.dup_vs_let_hashcons_counterexample). A tree-producing extractor such as Toy.DirCC.extract (on a different, Term-based e-graph type) would do exactly that.

evalTbl ignores the tag k of a frz node and keys choices by table slot; hashcons merges only syntactically identical nodes. Rewriting the argument of one copy of an inlined tagged freeze, even by an exact identity such as x0 + 0 to x0, makes the term not well-tagged, gives the copies separate slots, and lets the table produce an outcome the source cannot (Toy.DirCC.Dup.copy_rewrite_breaks_hashcons).

After inlining duplicates a tagged freeze, frz k is not refinement-monotone per copy under either the per-tag reading or the table reading: refining only the first copy's poison argument of frz0 x0 + frz0 x0 to 1 gives frz0 1 + frz0 x0, which can produce 1, while letProg produces only even numbers (Toy.DirCC.Dup.one_copy_refinement_breaks_tagged_sharing). Refinement under a tagged freeze must be applied to all copies at once; soundness of the simultaneous step is not stated here.
Toy.DirCC.Dup is a standalone expression language with no formal link to Toy.DirCC.Term, Model, Profile, Cert or EGraph.

The counterexample for UniqueTags refutes the direction indep -> hcSem (independent outcomes are lost by merging). Whether the direction hcSem -> indep holds without UniqueTags is not stated or proved here.
